en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Section on the Puzzles,
Chapter on Intimacy.
7. The Question of Ghaṭīkāra “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘The entire workshop of the potter Ghaṭīkāra remained roofless for three months, yet the gods did not send down rain.’”
Furthermore, it has been said:
“The hut of the Tathāgata Kassapa was leaking.
But why, venerable Nāgasena, does the hut of a Tathāgata who possesses such an abundance of roots of merit leak? Surely such power should be expected of a Tathāgata?
“Venerable Nāgasena, if the workshop of the potter Ghaṭīkāra was indeed rainproof and had a roof open to the sky, then the statement that ‘the hut of the Tathāgata leaked’ must be false.
If the hut of the Tathāgata leaked, then the statement that ‘the workshop of the potter Ghaṭīkāra was rainproof and had a roof open to the sky’ must also be false.
This too is a double-edged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.”
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘The entire workshop of Ghaṭīkāra the potter remained roofless for three months, yet the rain did not fall upon it.
And it was also said:”
‘The hut of the Tathāgata Kassapa is leaking.
Great King, the potter Ghaṭīkāra is virtuous, of lovely character, and has abundant roots of merit; he supports his blind and aged parents.
Without being present or having asked him for permission, [someone] took grass from his house for the Blessed One.

They covered the hut; through that act of gathering grass, he obtained an unshakable, immovable, well-composed, vast, and incomparable rapture, and he gave rise to even greater, immeasurable joy, thinking, "Oh, how well-entrusted is the Blessed One, the Supreme One in the World!
Through this, the result pertaining to the present life was produced for him.
For the Tathāgata, O Great King, does not waver through such a slight disturbance.

Just as Sineru, the king of mountains, does not tremble or shake even when struck by many hundreds of thousands of winds, and just as the great ocean, the most excellent of seas, is not filled nor undergoes any change even by many hundreds of thousands of millions of great Ganges rivers; so it is with the Tathāgata.
In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata does not waver because of such a minor disturbance.
However, Great King, when rain leaks into the Tathāgata’s hut, it is out of compassion for the great body of people.
Great King, seeing these two purposes, the Tathāgatas do not make use of requisites that have been prepared by themselves.
“Thinking, ‘This Teacher is the foremost one worthy of offerings,’ may gods and humans, by giving requisites to the Blessed One, be liberated from all miserable states;
and thinking, ‘Having displayed a miracle, they will seek a livelihood [for themselves],
lest others should criticize them’— perceiving these two benefits, the Tathāgatas do not partake of requisites created by themselves.”
“Great King, whether Sakka or Brahmā or you yourself were to make that hut proof against rain, that very act would be blameworthy, faulty, and subject to censure;
for these people, having made it appear as something extraordinary, delude the world and create an excess.
Therefore, that practice is to be avoided.”
“Great King, the Tathāgatas do not beg for material things; because they do not beg for material things, they are beyond reproach.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.
Thus ends the seventh dilemma, the Dilemma of Ghaṭīkāra.
